Lesson 13 (28/10) explanatory notes
Parts One and Two (Gigante and Bottazzi) built the foundations: how a fund works, the legal and fiscal
frameworks and the economics of VC contracts (preferred stock, liquidation preferences, option pools,
anti-dilution, down rounds). Part Three, taught by Marta Zava, follows the life cycle of a venture
investment and, above all, how to value it. This first lecture (28/10) sets the rules of the class and then
gives an umbrella: a macro picture of where money flows in Q3 2026, who gets it, who gets it back and
when. Market figures are not examinable (the professor said so explicitly): only the mechanisms the
numbers illustrate can be tested.

Course Logistics and the Exam
Three class rules: intervene (ask questions, bring news and cases), take ownership of your learning,
no loitering (attendance is not mandatory, so come to learn). There is no textbook: each content class
comes with slides with exercises, a separate solutions file and a ~20-page PDF of notes; solve the
exercises yourself before looking at the solutions. Cases are short and discussed in class. The
professor built an experimental AI exercise tool (on Claude) generating unlimited exercises with stepby-step solutions on the VC method, scorecard and Berkus, term-sheet mechanics and fund returns;
screenshot anything that does not add up. The syllabus was reordered so that the reasoning-heavy
topics (early-stage valuation, instruments such as the SAFE) come first, unicorns and exercises next,
fund raising, ecosystems and late-stage valuation/exits later. VC valuation is more art than science: at
seed you judge team and potential, not a balance sheet.
The exam (21 December 2026) combines multiple-choice questions (exactly one correct answer) and
short five-minute exercises. For this lecture: why a megaround changes how a fund invests, what a
power law is, why a big first-day jump signals underpricing, why LPs favour experienced managers,
why VC/GDP is fairer than absolute totals.

Record Dollars on a Narrow Base
The quarter in one sentence: record dollars at the top, scarce cash at the exit, a boom on paper and a
liquidity test in practice. Global VC in Q3 2026 was about $171bn, down ~28% quarter on quarter but
up ~43% year on year. This is not a contradiction: Q1 and Q2 were inflated by a few frontier-lab
rounds (one OpenAI round was $122bn of Q1's $317bn). Q3 had no such outlier, so it falls against Q2
while staying far above a normal quarter. Always ask which single deals sit behind a headline total.
Why 2021 is the benchmark. It was a record year (cheap companies after COVID, spectacular ecommerce and SaaS metrics, low rates) and there was a mechanical reason: a fund lives about ten
years (7 + 3) and has two to three years to deploy; management fees and carry only make sense if
capital is invested, so capital held back in 2020 was deployed in 2021. Uninvested commitments
create pressure to deploy, sometimes at high prices.
VC is not private equity. PE buys businesses unlikely to fail and improves them; 5–7x is excellent. In
VC about 8 companies out of 10 fail, so the winners must pay for the losses and a great outcome is
~100x. A solid company growing 20% a year is a good business but not VC material: a VC wants 100–
300x potential (perhaps 50–60x in Europe).

Concentration: AI, Megarounds and the Power Law
AI took about 64% of global VC dollars in Q3 (over four fifths in the US) but under half of the deals: a
higher share of value than of count simply means larger average rounds, not more deals. Such
concentration was never seen before (not with dot-com, SaaS or crypto). A megaround is a very large
round (often ≥ $100m; the extreme band is ≥ $1bn, 27 such rounds in one quarter, mostly AI labs and
compute): a few of them can move a whole quarter and lift the share of the country where they
happen.

In the US, deals of $100m+ were about 5% of deals but ~75% of value. A student called it Pareto; the

observations captures most of the total. It describes both the allocation of capital and returns: since
most companies fail, a fund must be built so that one or two outliers return the whole fund (early
ByteDance investors made about 3,000x).

From Spray-and-Pray to a Few Hands-On Bets
The classic answer to an 80% failure rate is diversification, spray-and-pray: a $40m fund writing
cheques of $0.5–1m, keeping reserves for follow-ons, has about 40 shots. It still fits the AI application
layer, where building a product is cheap. Megarounds break this logic: a fund cannot join a $200m
round with $1m (no company keeps a thousand investors on its cap table), so it puts in, say, $20m, half
the fund. Exposure is concentrated, so the manager has every incentive to be hands-on. The extreme
form is pre-team investing: funding star researchers with hundreds of millions before a team or
product exists. Through the professor's research lens of kingmaking, big rounds buy compute, talent

Who Gets Paid, and When: Exits, Underpricing and LPs
In 2026 capital is abundant but liquidity is scarce. Exits (the two successful ones are IPO and
M&A/trade sale) come in windows: when one opens you sell what you can before it closes. Listings
restarted in 2026, but in Q3 only 18 US VC-backed companies listed, none AI (mostly healthcare), and
the post-IPO record was poor: investors buy the story on day one and sell the numbers by day 120.

First-day underpricing = (Pclose, day 1 − Poffer) / Poffer

IPO proceeds = Poffer × shares sold in the primary offering

Worked example: the day-one pop
A company valued at $1bn sells 10% of its shares in the IPO at $1 per share (no selling
shareholders). On day one the price rises tenfold, so the traded shares are worth $1bn. The
company receives only the primary proceeds: 10% × $1bn = $100m. Underpricing = (10 − 1)/1 =
900%: about $900m of money left on the table goes to those who bought at the offer price.
Exam trap: a huge first-day gain does not prove the IPO was a success for the issuer; it measures
how badly the bank priced it. A rise of around 15% is normal and healthy. A higher secondary price
still helps (cheaper debt, more valuable remaining shares, better terms for later sales), but the cash
received is fixed at the offer price.

Secondaries, LP Flows and the Flight to Experience
Outside a couple of giant listings, liquidity came from strategic M&A and secondaries (LPs selling fund
stakes, GP-led continuation vehicles, tender offers). Secondaries now do the job IPOs used to do, but
at a price: LP stakes traded at about 80% of NAV, a ~20% haircut; companies that last raised at 2021
peaks sell at discounts of 60–90% to their last round. Net cash flow to LPs (distributions received
minus capital contributed) has been negative in the US by about $200bn since 2022: LPs
(endowments, pension funds, HNWIs, funds of funds; portfolio theory suggests a 6–10% allocation to
VC) fund the industry more than it pays them back. This is the DPI drought: paper returns (TVPI) are
back, cash returns (DPI) are not.
About 88% of US fundraising went to managers on Fund IV or later: an index of uncertainty, as LPs
back people who have already taken funds to maturity. Emerging managers are squeezed and the
industry becomes a barbell of megafunds and micro-funds. The chain to remember: no exits → no
distributions → cash-starved LPs → commitments concentrated on experienced managers and
stakes sold at a discount. The scarce resource is liquidity, not capital.

Boom or Bubble?
A bubble is a pricing error, not a verdict on the technology: prices run ahead of the cash flows that can
realistically justify them. A bubble can burst while the technology proves transformative: Amazon fell
from above $100 to about $6 after the dot-com crash and became dominant. The useful question is
who holds the risk when prices correct (funds, private credit, lenders financing the AI build-out). The
professor's personal view: early websites were billboards and the internet's real power came later;
today AI mostly substitutes existing functions, and she doubts LLMs will be the long-run paradigm.

Comparing Regions: VC over GDP
The top three markets are the US, Europe and China (Europe and China roughly a quarter of the US
each: a two-and-a-half-pole world); the fourth, Israel, is about ten times smaller than the third.
Absolute totals mostly reflect size: dividing by GDP or population turns a ranking of economies into a
ranking of venture intensity, the right lens to compare Israel with continental blocks. Ecosystems are
local: "US vs Europe" really means a few metropolitan hubs (the SF Bay Area alone took ~24% of
global dollars vs ~17% for all of Europe), and Delaware-registered companies should be assigned to
where they operate. Each ecosystem's VC feeds its dominant local industry (Silicon Valley software
and models, Boston biotech, New York finance, which is why New York briefly overtook the Valley via
fintech). European VC grew for eight quarters but on a few megarounds while deal counts fall;
champions raise at home and list in New York, so the gap is in listing venues and late-stage capital.
Italy shows the same pattern in miniature.

Deal Sourcing and Deal Screening
Lesson 14 (29/10, first part) explanatory notes
Lesson 13 described the market from the outside: a power law of returns, extreme concentration on AI,
megarounds. This lesson (first half of the double class of 29/10) steps inside a fund and follows a deal
in the order it travels: first it must reach the investor (sourcing), then survive a sequence of filters
(screening), and only then is it priced (early-stage valuation, started at the end and continued in
Lesson 15). The answer, built on the survey of Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan and Strebulaev (2020) and
its European counterparts: sourcing is above all a network activity, data tools change it without
replacing it, and screening is a process of exclusion and prioritization driven by the team, fit with the
fund and the plausibility of an outsized return. Exact figures are not tested (orders of magnitude and
directions are); the two five-minute exercises (funnel diagnosis, fit decision) are reproduced below.

Where Deals Come From
VCs buy equity in companies about which almost nothing can be verified, and founders know far more
than the investor. Three classic ideas frame the problem: Akerlof (1970), adverse selection (an
investor who cannot tell teams apart attracts the weak ones); Spence (1973), the informed party
reveals quality through signals costly to imitate (referrals, patents, prior exits); Knight (1921), risk
(estimable probabilities) vs uncertainty (not estimable), the realm of early-stage decisions. Deal flow is
the stream of opportunities reaching a fund: its quality matters more than its quantity, and depends on
the relationships through which it arrives.
Gompers et al. surveyed 885 VCs at 681 firms (data 2015–2016: the professor stressed that a 2020
paper reflects older data, so the directions hold but the 2% of quantitative sourcing is surely much
higher today). The average firm considered about 200 companies a year and closed about 4; partners
spent 22 of 55 weekly hours on sourcing and networking. 49% named deal selection as the main
source of value creation, 27% post-investment value added, 23% deal flow, but selection only works
on what sourcing brings in. Late-stage investors generate 42% of their deals themselves vs 23% for
early-stage ones.

Referrals, Proactive Search and the Network
What makes an e-mail worth reading is who sent it. A referral carries context (who the founders are,
why the deal fits), an implicit endorsement (the referrer chose this company) and a reputational

disproportionately from companies that could not get an introduction (Akerlof). Its value depends on
how well the referrer knows the company and the fund and what he stands to lose; check incentives (a

The channel is evidence, not a verdict: treat it as a prior and revise it. Time pressure ("the round
closes Friday") must never substitute for evidence. Proactive sourcing (conferences, academics,
relationships with prospective founders before they raise) gives informational and relational
advantages and makes access competitive and path-dependent: past success attracts better deals,

programs, universities, databases) trade exclusivity for coverage: everyone at a demo day sees the
same companies, which pushes prices up. The VC network (portfolio companies, serial entrepreneurs,
other VCs, LPs, experts, lawyers, acquirers) supplies information as well as deals: better-networked
firms (centrality in syndication networks) perform better (Hochberg, Ljungqvist and Lu 2007), and
absorptive capacity (Cohen and Levinthal 1990) speeds evaluation in familiar fields.
The professor's point from experience: sourcing is a small community (founders' dinners, enablers,
reciprocity among VCs; founders who failed well are backed again), and the network is how you verify
business reputation: she declined a deal after a trusted contact warned her the founder had scammed
a former partner, and checked it herself. Even a YC label or a demo-day lead needs someone who can
vouch for the person.

Data-Driven Sourcing: Algorithms Find, Humans Pick
Platforms monitor hiring, web traffic, launches, patents, code repositories and financing news: EQT's
Motherbrain (2016), SignalFire's Beacon, relationship-intelligence tools such as Affinity. They
automate first screening, rank companies on traction and timing, map who knows whom (so a datafound company can still get a warm introduction) and track sectors, promising wider coverage
(founders outside hubs) and earlier engagement. Limits: sparse data on the earliest companies,
herding (same signals → same companies → higher prices), team quality hard to measure, and, per
Bonelli (2025), data-adopting VCs pick start-ups similar to past ones better but are less likely to fund
the rare, genuinely novel outliers, a serious cost in a power-law world. In class: model the tails, not
the mean; data mislead (the best engineers may not be on LinkedIn); the human component remains,
because founders choose investors for value added, not money.

Selection Criteria: the Team First, but Not Alone
Asked for the single most important factor, 47% of US VCs named the management team (95% called
it important), more than three times any other; fit with the fund 14%, product 13%, business model
10%, market 8%, industry 6%; valuation (1%) and ability to add value (2%) almost never. Teams also
explain both successes (96%) and failures (92%). Europeans agree (93%) but focus more on
individual founders' passion and commitment, Americans on the team as a whole and fundamentals.
In the jockey vs horse debate, Kaplan, Sensoy and Strömberg (2009) followed 50 companies from
business plan to IPO: business lines stayed stable while management changed, so the horse looked
more durable. Practitioners still put the team first because before validation it is the main observable,
and it signals adaptability (fewer than 30% of companies meet projections). Factors are not
alternatives: a superb team where the fund cannot operate is still not an investment; what matters in
the business model is how the founders think about it; market and industry are summarised by the
TAM.
Italian survey (a former student, ~84 of ~120 VCs): more public VCs, many more early-stage and
healthcare investors, smaller funds, about double the deals per opportunity (less competition). The
professor "really did not like" that only ~1% named the TAM as top factor: many Italian VCs plan a
secondary sale to a PE fund, leaving the TAM to the buyer.

The Two Screening Questions: Fit and Return Potential
First, fit with the fund: stage, round and ticket size, industry, geography. Fit is a hard constraint, not
one criterion among many: LPs committed on the stated strategy, and investing outside it (style drift)
changes the risk profile they think they hold. It is also cheap to check (one e-mail reveals it), so it
comes first. Ticket size follows mechanically from fund size (Altamarea case):

Average first cheque = investable capital × (1 − reserve share) / number of companies = 100 × 0.45 / (35 to 40) ≈
€1.1–1.3m
(€120m fund, ~€100m investable after fees, ~55% reserved for follow-ons.) A company asking €100k
would not put enough money to work; one needing €20m next round needs more than the fund can
provide. Second, the potential for a substantial return: about a quarter of investments lose money and
only ~9% return more than 10x, so a deal capped at 2–3x adds little however likely; the question is
whether a large outcome is plausible. This requires sizing the opportunity, an independent evaluation
of key assumptions (internal consistency, not accounting compliance), risks, competition and the
team's adaptability and resources (relationships with suppliers, clients and acquirers carry over when
the product changes). Screening outputs a decision on how to allocate the team's time, not a
valuation.

Why DCF Fails Before Revenue
For a mature company, history (revenues, margins, investment) disciplines the forecast. For a prerevenue start-up there are no cash flows to extrapolate, the probability of failure is high but
unknown, successful outcomes are extremely skewed and founders' projections are systematically
optimistic: the inside view of Kahneman and Lovallo (1993), which neglects the base rates of
comparable ventures (Berkus: fewer than 1 start-up in 1,000 meets its projected revenues). A DCF
inherits this optimism and its precision to the dollar hides what is Knightian uncertainty, not risk: false
precision.
Practice agrees (Gompers et al. 2020): only 22% of VCs use NPV; 63% use the cash-on-cash
multiple and 42% the IRR; 31% of early-stage investors do not forecast cash flows at all, and 63% of
early-stage investors set the valuation from the amount invested and a target stake. Valuation is
driven by the anticipated exit, comparables and the desired ownership.

The VC Method (Sahlman and Scherlis 1987; Sahlman 1990) values a company by discounting its exit
value at the fund's target return and adjusting for dilution. Unlike the three present-evidence methods
it prices a future scenario, and it is the first that ties the entry price to the economics of the fund.
Steps: (1) exit value in year N (revenue or earnings × comparable multiple); (2) post-money = exit /
target multiple; (3) pre-money = post − investment; (4) required stake = I / post, adjusted for dilution.

The Unicorn Phenomenon
The term was coined by Aileen Lee (2013), when there were only 39 unicorns; it signalled rarity: Lee
counted US software companies founded since 2003 and valued at $1bn or more, about 0.07% of
venture-backed software start-ups (in class the professor added an early cap of ten employees, not in
the written chapter). Above $10bn a company is a decacorn, above $100bn a hectocorn. The key word
is private: most of the 2013 unicorns have left the list because they listed, were acquired or failed. By
Q1 2026 there were about 1,680 unicorns worth $8.6 trillion in aggregate post-money, distributed as a
power law (Anthropic ≈ $965bn, OpenAI and ByteDance the second trillion, then a long tail just above
$1bn; cross-holdings inflate the total). Status rests on the post-money of the latest round, updated
only when the company raises, so 51.2% are dormant (their mark predates the 2022 correction): no
new capital in over two years, because after the 2022 rate rises capital is scarce, the IPO window was
nearly shut and a new round could expose an inflated mark.
Three forces explain the rise: technology (Andreessen, 2011, "software is eating the world": near-zero
marginal costs, global distribution through cloud and mobile), market structure (network effects and
winner-take-most, so valuations grow convexly and ahead of profits) and speed (Play Bigger: firms
founded in the early 2010s reached high valuations about twice as fast as those of the early 2000s).
Firms also stay private longer: US listings roughly halved between 1996 and 2012 (the listing gap,
Doidge, Karolyi and Stulz, 2017), the fall in IPOs was concentrated among small firms, which often gain
more by selling to a larger company (Gao, Ritter and Zhu, 2013), and the 1996 NSMIA fuelled late-stage
private capital (Ewens and Farre-Mensa, 2020). Value once earned by IPO investors now accrues
privately, and price discovery happens in a few negotiated transactions. Uber is the flagship: founded
2009, about $50bn in 2016 with no profits, IPO in 2019 at $75.5bn, first full-year operating profit in
2023.

The Exit Landscape and the Dual Role of the IPO
A VC fund has a finite life (about ten years): value counts for LPs only when realized, so the prospect
of exit shapes every earlier decision. Of the five routes (IPO, M&A, secondary, buyback, write-off; see
Lesson 21), M&A dominates by count: 995 acquisitions vs 62 listings of US VC-backed firms in 2025
(PitchBook-NVCA, Q4 2025), yet the two had roughly equal total value. If totals are equal, the ratio of
averages is the inverse ratio of counts:

V̄ IPO / V̄ acq = (V/62) / (V/995) = 995/62 ≈ 16
The IPO has a dual role: it raises capital (primary shares: proceeds to the company, dilution for
holders) and starts a liquidity process (secondary shares: proceeds to the sellers, share count
unchanged); for the VC it is a partial liquidity event, not a full exit. Framing theories: Myers and Majluf
(1984) (equity from firms the market does not understand is discounted), Grossman and Hart (1980)
(silence reads as bad news, so disclosure is mandated), Megginson and Weiss (1991) (VCs and banks
certify), Loughran and Ritter (1995) (IPOs cluster in hot markets).

The US Process: S-1, SEC Review, Bookbuilding
The Securities Act of 1933 (Section 5: no offer before filing, no sale before the registration is
effective) and the Exchange Act of 1934 create a disclosure regime: risky shares may be sold if
investors are told what they need. The Form S-1 contains the prospectus (risk factors, use of
proceeds, dilution, MD&A, audited US GAAP accounts). Since the JOBS Act (2012) emerging growth
companies may file a confidential draft and test the waters (extended to all issuers in 2017–2019),
filing publicly 15 days before the roadshow. The SEC sends comment letters, the issuer files S-1/A
amendments, and the statement is declared effective on pricing day. Effectiveness is not an
endorsement (Section 23); credibility comes from liability: Section 11 makes the issuer strictly liable,
while directors, underwriters and auditors have a due diligence defense.
In a firm-commitment underwriting the syndicate buys at the offer price minus the gross spread and
resells: test the waters → roadshow (red herring with a price range) → book of demand → pricing the
evening before trading, with discretionary allocation. Benveniste and Spindt (1989): allocations of
underpriced shares reward investors for revealing demand, so underpricing is the cost of information;
hence partial adjustment (Hanley 1993): deals priced above the range are raised too little and pop
most.
